hooks.text: A structure three billion light-years long should not exist.
Can a single cosmic structure span one-fifteenth of the visible universe?
Gravity is too slow to have built the universe's largest structure.

title: The Megastructure That Breaks Physics
description: Astronomers discovered a galaxy crescent so large that gravity shouldn't have had time to build it.

beats.text: A structure three billion light-years long should not exist.
beats.visual: Sloan Digital Sky Survey 3D map of galaxies.
queries: large scale structure of the universe

beats.text: In 2021, student Alexia Lopez was mapping distant light in the constellation Boötes.
beats.visual: Star map of the constellation Boötes.

beats.text: She analyzed magnesium two absorption lines, using ultra-bright quasars as giant lamps to illuminate hidden matter.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of a quasar's light beam through gas clouds.

beats.text: Using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, Lopez found a colossal crescent of galaxies stretching 3.3 billion light-years across.
beats.visual: Scientific plot of the Giant Arc galaxy distribution.

beats.text: This Giant Arc is so massive it spans one-fifteenth the radius of the entire observable universe.
beats.visual: Diagram showing the Giant Arc within the observable universe.

beats.text: Standard cosmology says gravity cannot form structures larger than 1.2 billion light-years.
beats.visual: Illustration of the theoretical 1.2 billion light-year size limit.

beats.text: There simply hasn't been enough time since the Big Bang for something this big to clump together.
beats.visual: Simulation of cosmic structures forming after the Big Bang.

beats.text: This gargantuan galaxy cluster suggests that our basic understanding of the universe is actually broken.
beats.visual: Photograph of researcher Alexia Lopez at the University of Central Lancashire.
